items.prompt: A vending machine drops the drink every time, but gives no sign it took your coin. What failed?
choices: The communication with the person
The motor that drops the drink down
The coin reader inside the machine
items.explanation: The machine works; it just never says so, so the person is left guessing.

items.prompt: Which question checks usability rather than correctness?
choices: Does the request return a success code?
Can the person tell what is happening?
Does every field pass validation?
items.explanation: Usability is about what the person can perceive and do, not about whether the code ran.

items.prompt: A save always succeeds but nothing on screen changes. Is the feature usable?
choices: Yes, because the save itself succeeded
Yes, because no error ever appeared
No, the person cannot tell it worked
items.explanation: Success the person cannot see is, for them, indistinguishable from failure.

items.prompt: What does a passing test suite tell you?
choices: The code matches what was specified
The screen is easy to understand
The screen is easy for a person to understand
items.explanation: Tests check behavior against a specification, not the person's experience.

items.prompt: Why do people press a silent button repeatedly?
choices: They enjoy pressing the button just for fun
They cannot tell the first press registered
The button is physically broken inside
items.explanation: Without feedback, repeating the action is the only way to test whether it worked.

items.prompt: Usability heuristics are best described as
choices: Laws that every single screen must obey to the letter
A catalogue of approved interface widgets
Rules of thumb for diagnosing communication gaps
items.explanation: They are diagnostic lenses, not laws and not a pattern library.

items.prompt: Which is a usability failure even though nothing crashed?
choices: A button gives no sign it was pressed
A server returns an error code on load
A page takes a long time to be built
items.explanation: The failure is in the exchange with the person, not in the code path.

items.prompt: Who is the best judge of whether a screen communicates well?
choices: The person who wrote all of the code
Watching a person try to use it
The automated test report from the build
items.explanation: Only a person's experience shows whether the exchange works.

items.prompt: A team ships a form whose every request succeeds, and support is flooded with 'did it save?' tickets. What does this show?
choices: Correctness and usability are separate, and only the first was verified
The backend has an intermittent bug that the tests simply did not manage to cover
The tickets come from people who skipped the written instructions
The tests need higher coverage before the next release goes out
items.explanation: Tickets about uncertainty, not about wrong results, point to a communication gap. Tests cannot see it.
items.reference:
Two separate axes
correctness: does it do what it was built to do?
usability: can the person tell what it is doing and recover?
a test suite checks only the first
Why: a feature can pass every test and still leave the person guessing.
items.learnMore:
Correctness vs. usability

Correctness is a property of the code against its specification. Usability is a property of the exchange between the interface and a person. Passing tests proves the first and says nothing about the second.

Common mistake

Assuming no bug reports means no usability problem. People often just walk away or ask for help.
items.reflection: Think of a tool at home that works perfectly but that you never quite trust. What does it fail to tell you?

items.prompt: Which finding would be a usability problem rather than a correctness bug?
choices: An export writes the wrong column order into the saved file
A correct export finishes with no message, so people start it twice
An export crashes outright whenever the chosen file name contains a slash character
An export silently drops the last row of the data it writes
items.explanation: Only the first case has correct output and a failed exchange. The others are wrong behavior.

Visibility of system status
Help and documentation

items.prompt: A delete with no undo breaks which heuristic?

Aesthetic and minimalist design
User control and freedom

choices: Recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
User control and freedom, for backing out
Flexibility and efficiency of use
items.explanation: A bare code names no problem and offers no next step.

items.prompt: Why name the violated heuristic?
choices: It makes the review take a good deal longer
It makes the complaint specific and fixable
It shows that the screen is simply illegal
items.explanation: A named gap points to a concrete design change.

items.prompt: Silent save is a problem of
choices: Jargon words
Clutter
Feedback
items.explanation: Feedback is visibility of system status.

items.prompt: Which phrase is a heuristic name?
choices: Error prevention
Make it pop
Looks old-fashioned
items.explanation: Heuristics are the standard named lenses, not taste words.

items.prompt: A screen speaks in database terms. Which heuristic is broken?
choices: Error prevention before the action is taken
Match between system and the real world
Help and documentation
items.explanation: The language belongs to the engineer, not the person.

items.prompt: How many heuristics can one bad screen violate?
choices: Never more than one
Exactly three
Several at once
items.explanation: A single missing design decision often breaks several at the same point.

items.prompt: A person deletes a record by accident and the page offers no way back. Which heuristic does this primarily violate?
choices: Visibility of system status, because the record vanished silently
User control and freedom, because there is no exit from the mistake
Consistency and standards, because delete looks like other buttons
Error prevention, because nothing stopped the click before it landed
items.explanation: The missing way back is user control and freedom. Prevention would be a separate, earlier fix.
items.reference:
Complaint to heuristic
no feedback after Save: visibility of system status
delete with no undo: user control and freedom
raw ERR_402: recognize, diagnose, recover from errors
Why: naming the heuristic turns 'this feels clunky' into a specific, fixable change.
items.learnMore:
Naming the failure

A vague complaint ('clunky') gives a designer nothing to change. A named heuristic points at a missing capability: feedback, an exit, a plain-language message.

Common mistake

Naming the symptom ('the dialog is annoying') instead of the cause ('the user cannot tell what will be deleted').

items.prompt: How many heuristics are in the full list?
choices: Ten
Five
Twenty
items.explanation: Ten heuristics, grouped here into five questions.

items.prompt: Which pair of heuristics shares one question in the five-question grouping?

items.explanation: Both reduce the work of relearning or remembering, so both ask whether the interface stays predictable.
items.reference:
Ten heuristics, five questions
talk to the user: 1 status, 2 real-world match
stay in control: 3 control and freedom, 7 flexibility
stay predictable: 4 consistency, 6 recognition
protect against mistakes: 5 prevention, 9 recovery
no more complex than needed: 8 minimalism, 10 help
Why: grouping by what each protects makes ten rules easy to run through a screen.
items.learnMore:
Why group them

Grouping is a memory and review aid. During a critique you ask five questions rather than recite ten names.

Common mistake

Treating the groups as official Nielsen categories. They are a teaching grouping of his ten.
items.reflection: Pick a product you use daily. Which of the five questions does it answer best, and which worst?

Both assume the interface must serve more than one kind of user and speed
items.explanation: Safety nets suit the uncertain, shortcuts suit the fluent. One interface serves both.

Names no problem and no next step
Takes too long to appear after the failure

Documentation
Feedback

items.reference:
Feedback and plain language
status: spinner, checkmark, progress bar
real-world match: 'cart', not 'session-scoped order buffer'
errors: plain language, the precise problem, a next step
Why: the interface owes the person a model of what is happening that matches their own.
items.learnMore:
Feedback and errors

Silence, jargon and bare codes fail alike: the system has the information and the person has to guess. Feedback can be light, as long as it exists.

Common mistake

Thinking feedback is only for failures. Success the person cannot see is also a gap.

Prevention
Consistency

items.explanation: New information gives the person something to notice.

It always uses the wrong color for danger
People click through it on reflex
items.explanation: It adds a step without adding information.

choices: No, some causes lie outside the interface
Yes, if the designer adds enough dialogs

items.prompt: A plain-language failure message is part of
choices: Prevention
Recovery
Minimalism
items.explanation: It helps the person get past a failure that happened.

items.prompt: Eliminating an error-prone condition is
choices: A form of recovery from the mistake
A form of documentation
The strongest form of prevention
items.explanation: If the mistake cannot occur, nothing needs fixing.

items.prompt: A delete flow has an 'Are you sure? Yes/No' dialog on every action. Why might it still fail its purpose?
choices: Repeated generic prompts are clicked through without reading
Dialogs are slower to complete than inline buttons on mobile screens
Yes/No pairs are less readable than OK/Cancel pairs on any screen
Users strongly prefer actions that finish with no interruption at all
items.explanation: A prompt that adds no new information trains reflex clicking, so it catches nothing.
items.reference:
Two layers, in order
1. eliminate the error-prone condition
2. check and confirm, naming the consequence
3. recover: undo, plain error, restore path
Why: prevention is cheaper but cannot cover everything, so recovery is the fallback.
items.learnMore:
Prevention and recovery

Prevention acts before the mistake and is usually cheapest. Recovery acts after and covers causes the interface cannot control, like a payment declined elsewhere.

Common mistake

Treating a generic 'Are you sure?' as prevention. A confirmation people click through on reflex prevents nothing.
items.reflection: Think of a mistake you made recently that an interface could have stopped. Would prevention or recovery have helped more?

Logging the click so that someone can review it later on
items.explanation: Removing the possibility beats asking the person to notice it.

items.prompt: A toast with Undo after removal supports
choices: Visibility of system status
Consistency and standards
Help and documentation
items.explanation: It reports what just happened and offers a way back.

items.prompt: A recently-removed list with Restore supports
choices: Minimalism in the layout
User control and freedom
Flexibility
items.explanation: It offers recovery after the undo window closes.

items.prompt: An admin-visible audit log supports
choices: Error prevention before the click lands
Aesthetic and minimalist design of the page
Recognizing and diagnosing what happened
items.explanation: It turns 'I think I did something' into a clear record.

items.prompt: Why can one heuristic appear twice in an audit?
choices: Its requirement holds at more than one point
The audit contains a mistake in its table of findings
Heuristics repeat in every list of findings
items.explanation: User control matters before and after the mistake.

items.prompt: The best confirmation text names
choices: Only the word Remove in bold type
The billing-admin role being removed
The product version and release date
items.explanation: That is the fact that would have stopped the incident.

items.prompt: Hover-only controls are risky because
choices: They load much more slowly than buttons
They look old-fashioned next to modern icons
They vanish for keyboard and touch users
items.explanation: A visible path must still exist.

items.prompt: Did the five fixes need new removal logic?
choices: No, only an audit record and a soft-delete window
Yes, a whole new backend service is required
Yes, a new type of database must be added
items.explanation: Only the communication around the operation changed.

items.prompt: A team adds a good confirmation dialog and considers the Remove button fixed. What does the audit say is still missing?
choices: Nothing, since the dialog covers the control heuristic completely
A restore path and a record, since the dialog can be clicked through
A larger button, so that the confirmation is easier to hit with a cursor on a small screen
A shorter confirmation text, so that there is less friction
items.explanation: Confirmation covers one moment. Discovery later needs a restore path and a log.
items.reference:
One click, five failures
before: error prevention
at the click: user control and freedom
right after: visibility of system status
later: user control and freedom (recovery)
escalation: recognize, diagnose, recover
Why: one missing design decision breaks several heuristics at different points in time.
items.learnMore:
Auditing along the timeline

Walk the flow backward from the incident and ask at each point which heuristic governs it. The same heuristic can appear twice because its requirement holds before and after the mistake.

Common mistake

Fixing only the moment of the click. A confirmation does not replace a restore path, and a toast does not replace an audit log.
items.reflection: Take a recent mistake you made in some app and walk it along the timeline: before, during, right after, later. Where could it have been caught?

items.prompt: In the audit table, which fix addresses 'the admin cannot point to what happened' when escalating to support?
choices: A toast shown on screen right after the removal
A confirmation that names the role of the removed user
An admin-visible log of who removed whom and when
A hover-only trash icon placed on each member row
items.explanation: Escalation needs a record the admin can see, not a backend log only engineers read.

The toast covers only seconds, and regret can come days later

Not knowing the removal happened

items.explanation: Raising the cost of a destructive action relative to routine ones prevents careless misclicks.

items.prompt: In the model, what does each added step cost a routine removal?
choices: About 4 seconds
About 40 seconds
Nothing
items.explanation: Time grows from 3 s by 4 s per step.

items.prompt: In the model, accidents with zero added steps were about
choices: 4 per 1,000 clicks
41 per 1,000 clicks
410 per 1,000 clicks
items.explanation: The curve starts at 41 and falls with each step.

items.prompt: Which action deserves a confirmation?
choices: Renaming a tag in a shared list
Changing the sort order of a table
Revoking someone's billing access
items.explanation: It is destructive and hard to reverse.

items.prompt: Renaming a tag usually needs
choices: No confirmation, since it is easy to reverse
A typed confirmation of the person's full name
Three separate confirmation steps in a row
items.explanation: Low-stakes, reversible actions should stay quick.

items.prompt: Confirmation fatigue means
choices: Prompts stop loading after several repeated uses
People click through prompts without reading
People read each prompt twice before acting
items.explanation: Overused prompts stop preventing anything.

items.prompt: Silent auto-save of a draft is
choices: Always a violation
Illegal on mobile
Usually fine
items.explanation: Low stakes and reversible, so light feedback is enough.

items.prompt: Heuristics are best treated as
choices: Trade-offs to balance by stakes
Dials to be turned to the maximum setting
Items to skip
items.explanation: Setting depends on stakes and reversibility.

items.prompt: Is the demo a measured study?
choices: Yes, it was measured with real users
No, an illustrative model
Yes, it comes from a large survey
items.explanation: It shows the shape of a trade-off only.

items.prompt: In the model, going from 3 to 4 confirmation steps changes accidents from 4 to 2 per 1,000 and adds 4 seconds. What does this suggest?
choices: Four steps is the right number for every kind of action in every product
Accidents can never be reduced below 2 per 1,000 clicks
Later steps save little for the same time cost, so more is not better
The time cost per step shrinks as more steps are added
items.explanation: The first step saves 24 per 1,000 for the same 4 seconds. Returns diminish.
items.reference:
Model: friction vs. accidents
0 steps: 41 accidents per 1,000, 3 s per routine removal
1 step: 17 per 1,000, 7 s
2 steps: 8 per 1,000, 11 s
4 steps: 2 per 1,000, 19 s
Why: each step costs the same time but saves fewer accidents, so friction should scale with stakes.
items.learnMore:
Proportional friction

The demo is an illustrative model, not a measured study. Its shape matters: steep early gains, flat later gains, and a constant time cost per step.

Common mistake

Reading the model's numbers as real rates. They illustrate a trade-off, not a finding.
items.reflection: Think of an action you do often that asks for confirmation. Is it worth the friction, and how would you decide?

items.prompt: A product removes confirmations from everything except account deletion to avoid fatigue. What does the criterion in the unit say is missing?
choices: A larger font on the account-deletion dialog, and nothing else changed
A shorter wording for the one remaining dialog
A shared timer applied across all confirmations
An action-by-action look at stakes and reversibility
items.explanation: Remove-member and delete-workspace may also be destructive and hard to reverse.

Prevention against recovery in destructive flows
Consistency against flexibility for expert users
Documentation against recognition in a help panel
items.explanation: Blanket feedback clutters. Visibility should scale with stakes and reversibility.

items.prompt: Which design best applies 'friction proportional to consequence'?
choices: The same dialog on every action, for the sake of consistency
A named confirmation for removing admins and none for renaming tags
No dialogs anywhere, relying on undo alone to catch every possible mistake
A typed confirmation on every action across the product
items.explanation: Matching friction to stakes avoids both the missing guard and the reflex click-through.
